title: Valid Palindrome
description:
A string is a palindrome if it reads the same forwards and backwards once you **ignore case** and **drop every character that is not a letter or digit**.

Given `s`, return `true` if it is a palindrome under those rules, otherwise `false`. A string with no alphanumeric characters at all counts as a palindrome.

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

examples.explanation: Nothing is left after filtering, and the empty string is a palindrome.

hints: Building a cleaned, lower-cased copy and comparing it to its reverse works in O(n) extra space. Can you avoid the copy?
Walk two indices inward from both ends, skipping anything that is not alphanumeric.
Compare `s[i].lower()` with `s[j].lower()` only when both point at alphanumerics; mismatch means not a palindrome. Stop when the indices cross.

approach:
**Two pointers converging from the ends.** Skip non-alphanumeric characters on each side, then compare the two characters case-insensitively. Any mismatch is a definitive no; if the pointers cross without one, the string is a palindrome.

**Why it works:** a string is a palindrome iff the k-th character from the front equals the k-th from the back for all k, and skipping filtered characters on both sides preserves that correspondence in the cleaned string without materialising it.

**Common mistakes:** forgetting the `i < j` guard inside the skip loops (index runs off the end on inputs like `"!!!"`); treating digits as non-alphanumeric (`"0P"` is not a palindrome because `0` and `p` differ); the one-liner `cleaned == cleaned[::-1]` is accepted but uses O(n) extra space, so mention the trade-off.

**Interview follow-ups:** Allow deleting at most one character (Valid Palindrome II: on mismatch try skipping either side). Find the longest palindromic substring (expand around centres). Check a linked list for a palindrome in O(1) space (reverse the second half).
